Definition — Jacobian
      
        For $f=(f_1,\dots,f_m):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$, $J_f(x)\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ has entries $\partial f_i/\partial x_j$; row $i$ is $\nabla f_i^{\top}$. If every $f_i$ is differentiable at $x$ (e.g. $f$ is $C^1$ near $x$), then $f(x+\delta)=f(x)+J_f(x)\delta+e(\delta)$ with $\|e(\delta)\|/\|\delta\|\to0$: the Jacobian is the best local linear map. Existing entries alone do not give this (the Pitfall above has $J_f(0)=0$, yet $f=\tfrac12$ on the diagonal). For scalar $f$, $J_f=\nabla f^{\top}$. An affine map $Wx+b$ has $J=W$; an elementwise activation $\sigma(v)$ has $J=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma'(v_1),\dots,\sigma'(v_n))$. Example: $f=(x_1x_2,\ x_1+x_2^2)$ has $J_f=\begin{bmatrix}x_2 & x_1\\ 1 & 2x_2\end{bmatrix}$, equal to $\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1\\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}$ at $(1,2)$.
